b: The 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship also began on November 24, but Titled Tuesday continued apace, with its ongoing role in qualification for one of next year's biggest chess competitions, the 2027 Esports World Cup (EWC). GM Hikaru Nakamura won, scoring 9.5/11 for the victory on tiebreaks ahead of GMs Alireza Firouzja and Andrey Esipenko.
Nakamura widened his already substantial lead in the 2026-27 Champions Chess Tour (CCT) Standings with the victory, which was his third of the year but his second in just the last six weeks.
Game And Move Of The Day

In addition to their points from Titled Tuesday, Nakamura and GM Denis Lazavik also have at least 30 points from victories in the first round of Speed Chess Championship XI. More are possible if they advance farther, and some other players will also get extra points as SCC matches continue.
Unlike last year's CCT events, top finishers in the SCC and Chess.com Open aren't guaranteed a spot in the EWC beyond what their points entitle them to. The top 12 qualify.

There was no Chess.com broadcast of Titled Tuesday this week because of the world championship. Nakamura streamed on his Kick channel and then recapped game one of the world championship for YouTube; the latter is below.

Nakamura was in fine playing form early after some small difficulty in the first round, becoming one of 14 players on 4/4. Firouzja and Esipenko had achieved the same score. Among Nakamura's victories was an underpromotion in the third round that induced instant resignation from FM Yan Domin after just 21 moves.

While Nakamura lost in the fifth round to IM Renato Terry, Esipenko and Firouzja's success continued in the next round. Firouzja defeated GM Bardiya Daneshvar with the devastating 31.Nf6+. As Domin could only do against Nakamura's last move of round three, Daneshvar resigned.

By now, just six perfect players remained, and that number would dwindle to two by the end of round six, after Terry and Firouzja made a draw. Terry played a great game, but slipped near the end to allow perpetual check. The players to successfully reach 6/6 were Esipenko and, after a bizarre blunder by his opponent, IM Kirill Klukin.
Naturally, they were matched up in the seventh round, where Esipenko got to play White and won cleanly, without any need for dramatics.

Elsewhere, Firouzja just needed 19 moves to get back into the win column against IM Pawel Sowinski, while the near-opposite happened in Terry's game as he lost a time scramble against GM Jose Martinez. Meanwhile, Nakamura kept his recovery going with a second straight win, while GM Fabiano Caruana pulled off his sixth in a row to join Firouzja and Martinez on 6.5/7.

To defend his perfect score, Esipenko now had to face Firouzja, but did get White. Caruana had White versus Martinez, and Nakamura was back up to board three against GM Ray Robson. The Esipenko–Firouzja game concluded bloodlessly, allowing the perfect score bounty to survive yet another tournament unscathed and move to $6,750 next week. Over in the Americas, Caruana seemed to be heading for a win, but Martinez took it from him in time trouble, while Nakamura was struggling to the point of referring to himself in the third person, but Robson soon was the one to run out of time.

That left Martinez and Esipenko the only players on 7.5/8 entering the final break of the tournament. Martinez would end up getting the better of their matchup coming out of it, advancing into the sole lead. Behind him, however, Nakamura and Firouzja kept up the pressure and reached 8/9. Against FM Artin Ashraf, Nakamura missed a mate-in-one, but was so far ahead it didn't matter, while Firouzja soundly defeated GM Zhamsaran Tsydypov.

Nakamura and Firouzja both faced tough matches in the 10th round, taking Black against Martinez and Caruana, respectively. Yet both won, making themselves coleaders with one round to go. Nakamura credited himself with an "impressive squeeze" to get the win out of a position that looked drawn for some time, and knock Martinez from his perch.

Espying his tiebreaks, Nakamura was pessimistic about his winning chances, especially after he took the black pieces in his final round. Because of the latter fact, Nakamura played cautiously, and an extremely uneventful draw followed. But Nakamura's tiebreaks were closer than he thought, and the draw put him on the brink of winning.
Esipenko, facing Terry with both of them on 8.5 points, was already up 51 seconds on the clock when Terry took another 38 ticks to play the losing move.

Martinez also had a chance to move up to 9.5 points, but he could only stalemate GM Sina Movahed. Nine points were still enough to finish fourth with better tiebreaks than two IMs, Aleksandr Usov in fifth and Havard Haug in sixth.

Nakamura assumed he hadn't won until the end-of-tournament standings popped up on his screen; he ultimately beat out Firouzja by two tiebreak points and Esipenko by six. Nakamura readily admitted to improved play in recent Titled Tuesdays, which he credited to two things: playing more serious openings and using more time judiciously (instead of playing quickly and, his words, "trying to cheese on the clock" at the end of games). The new strategies are clearly helping, and his presence at the 2027 Esports World Cup is already nearly assured.
